summary: We built a mobile-friendly storytelling website that introduces school-age space fans to ten NASA machines left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space, from Apollo moon buggies to Voyager 1. Each machine has a story, the science it made possible, and a fun fact, with a status badge showing whether it is silent, still working, or still travelling. A live Voyager 1 distance counter, a timeline and a quiz make it interactive. It answers the challenge by turning old hardware into characters kids care about, and shows why exploration data still matters today.
details:
What it does: Visitors explore 10 mission stories, filter them by Moon, Mars or deep space, and open each one to read the story, the science and a fun fact. A live counter estimates Voyager 1's distance from Earth and its signal time, and a timeline and 4-question quiz reinforce learning.
How it works: It is a single responsive web page. Mission data is stored in JavaScript, and the cards, filters and quiz are generated from it. It works on phones and desktops, supports light and dark mode, and respects reduced-motion settings.
Benefits: It makes mission history easy for young learners and shows that finished missions still produce science.
Goal: To inspire students to see NASA's retired machines as explorers worth remembering.
Tools: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Canvas (starfield), PowerPoint for the demo deck.
dataRefs: NASA mission pages on science.nasa.gov for Apollo, Viking, Spirit, Opportunity, Ingenuity, InSight, Pioneer 10, Voyager and New Horizons; NASA’s Voyager mission status page (voyager.jpl.nasa.gov); NASA Image and Video Library (images.nasa.gov).
